articles.title: The price of what low-skilled workers know
articles.summary: It is heartening to see Indian workers helping generate the data that will drive the next generation of robots and artificial intelligence. Every month, a fresh batch of images does the rounds on LinkedIn and X: Indian factory employees with cameras strapped to their heads, their every movement recorded to train AI systems. The message? Tasks once thought resistant to automation are suddenly within AI’s reach. But these images of Indian workers wearing cameras should provoke something more serious than technological excitement or dystopian alarm. They should provoke a strategic question: Who owns data? Who builds models? Who controls these machines, and where does the resulting value accumulate?The instinctive reaction, of course, is enthusiasm, and these images are easy to celebrate. Yes, AI training is happening in India, and Indian workers are part of it. Gig, factory, and service workers are capturing ordinary physical tasks from a first-person perspective, and thousands of hours of Indian movement are becoming training material for the next generation of AI. Participation is not however synonymous with power. The important question to ask is not whether artificial intelligence is being trained in India. It’s what India is contributing to the process, on what terms, and who will ultimately own the productive assets created from it.Also read | Your boss may soon know what you’re asking Claude to do at workSeveral reports show that filming factory workers is fast becoming normal across Indian cities. In Gurugram and Nagpur, for example, workers are being recorded as they sew, adjust loom tension, and clear machine jams, or are simply under surveillance as they work. Similar data collection is spreading across the service economy. Human Archive, a Silicon Valley-based physical AI data startup, says it has deployed more than 1,000 headsets through partners in India and pays a base rate of $1 an hour for egocentric data collection, acknowledging that its Indian network helps keep compensation lower. Put simply, India’s cheap labour is becoming cheap machine-training data, too.The ambitions extend far beyond individual experiments and individual startups. EgoLab, an Indian startup which has been collecting first-person footage from Indian factories, was acquired in 2026 by US-registered Build Artificial Intelligence Inc. EgoLab's own material, reviewed by scroll had described their ambition to collect $100 million in footage from 100 million factory workers across major Indian states and sectors, including textiles, automobiles, chemicals, electronics, FMCG, and steel. BuildAI's published current roadmap similarly includes an ego-centric 100-million-dataset target for October 2027.These are not outcomes, but these ambitions reveal the intended scale of how India's data is being converted into a dataset that can be aggregated, transferred, and used globally. A worker wearing a camera records two outputs. The immediate output is the product of labour and information about how that labour is performed. In the future AI economy, the work is just not generating output; it is also recording the work, which can generate capital in the future.Also read | Zoho’s Sridhar Vembu sees a painful rebalancing of jobs in the AI ageThis is very relevant for a country where 88% of the workers are employed in occupations classified as low competency. This classification may make sense within the conventional labour market, but the same task has become extraordinarily valuable from the perspective of physical AI. Large language models could learn from vast stores of digitized text, images, and code; Physical AI there is no equivalent archive for much of what humans know about operating in the real world. Robotic Machines still struggle with actions people perform almost automatically: adjusting grips and pressure, manipulating unfamiliar objects, coordinating hands and tools, recovering from mistakes, and adapting when physical, emotional, and other conditions change. Therefore, what is routine knowledge for a human worker can become frontier knowledge for a machine. India's workforce is not only a source of inexpensive labour; it is also a potentially enormous reservoir for the demonstration that physical AI still needs to learn how the world works. However, a country that built its IT boom on labour-cost arbitrage, in practice, introduces a striking inversion: cheaper labour once reduced the incentive to automate. Now, if human demonstration can also be acquired cheaply, low wages may also help reduce the cost of teaching automation itself.In other words, India’s cheap labour no longer simply competes with automation. It could also cut the global cost of training robots and large language models. The point to contemplate is not merely whether machines will displace workers. It’s whether the knowledge workers bring becomes a strategic resource whose value is realised elsewhere. History isn’t reassuring here and we know that economies that supplied essential raw materials often had little control over the industries built around them, and their competitiveness suffered. That’s why Frank Herbert’s Dune offers such a valuable metaphor.In Dune, Arrakis, a barren desert planet, possesses spice, the indispensable resource on which an advanced civilisation relies for interstellar travel. However, owning this resource does not automatically mean dominance over the system built around it. Instead, others coordinate its extraction, trade, and conversion into power. India faces a version of that dilemma in the emerging physical AI economy. Its spice is the vast stock of embodied knowledge held by its workers - the accumulated judgement, dexterity, and experience in how tasks are performed. Indian companies can collect and annotate worker data but risk missing out on valuable layers if India remains just a raw knowledge supplier, as key datasets, models, robotics, software, platforms, and machines are mainly owned elsewhere. India is repeating an old development pattern in a new technological form.India’s previous outsourcing boom was built on supplying labour to the West. Physical AI raises the prospect that India will now also supply the knowledge embedded in that labour, captured as data and used to train robots, machines, and large language models worldwide. The strategic challenge for India, then, is to make sure it doesn’t remain merely the source of that input. That means guarding its data privacy and sovereignty, while also developing its own models, robotic capabilities, and intellectual property built on that data.India doesn’t need to stop the flow of spice. It just needs to make sure it doesn’t become merely Arrakis.(Amit Kapoor is chair & Sheen Zutshi isresearch manager atInstitute for Competitiveness.).

articles.summary:

Tilak has built a reputation of being a chase master over the last 12 months. Even in the second T20I against New Zealand, he pulled off a tense chase batting alongside Nitish Reddy. India have taken an unassailable 3-0 lead in the five-match series.
"I already had the power game; I have scored runs at number three as well. Now, batting at number five or six, I think about going for a boundary off the very first ball only if it's there to be hit," he said ahead of the fourth T20I here.
"Otherwise, I focus on taking the game deep. I take a bit more time. Initially, I focus on singles and doubles, finding gaps for fours or two runs," he added.

The losses were primarily driven by moderation in passenger traffic growth, rising aviation turbine fuel (ATF) prices and forex losses arising from the sharp depreciation of the Indian rupee, it said.
The onset of the war in West Asia in late February 2026 is expected to dampen air passenger traffic growth in FY27, ICRA said.
Additionally, increased costs due to depreciation of the Indian Rupee against the US dollar, elevated ATF prices and a rise in lease rentals amid continued aircraft deliveries are projected to cause a net loss of Rs 36,000-38,000 crore in this fiscal.
These cost escalations may not be adequately passed on to passengers through fare hikes, it said.

articles.title: EPFO plans to invest in startups, AIFs
articles.summary: The Employees Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) is working on guidelines to enable investments in alternative investment funds (AIFs), five years after the government cleared the retirement body’s entry into these high-growth asset classes and startups, The Times of India reported on Thursday.The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) discussed a proposal to allocate up to 3% of EPFO’s fresh annual accretions to Category I and Category II AIFs at an investment committee meeting last Thursday, the report said.The move could mark a shift in how the retirement fund body deploys workers’ savings, allowing it to gain exposure to startups and other growth-oriented investments beyond its traditional debt instruments.The proposal will now be placed before the central board of trustees, headed by Labour Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, in November, according to the report.The development follows a September letter from the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) seeking EPFO’s participation in the recently launched Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0.The proposal prompted discussions on a broader framework for investments in AIFs, the report added.Initially, EPFO is considering routing investments through institutional entities such as the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) and the Small Industries Development Bank of India’s (SIDBI) Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0.Under the investment pattern notified by the finance ministry, EPFO can invest up to 5% of its fresh accretions in asset-backed and trust-structured investments. It has not yet invested in SEBI-regulated Category I and Category II AIFs.Category I AIFs typically support startups, small businesses, infrastructure and venture capital, while Category II funds include private equity, real estate and private debt funds.The proposed framework includes safeguards such as a minimum AIF corpus of Rs 100 crore, limits on exposure to individual funds, restrictions on investments in foreign-incorporated entities and requirements for fund manager independence.EPFO manages around Rs 30 lakh crore in retirement savings for nearly 30 crore members, the report said.

articles.title: Rajnath Singh strengthens JAI partnership
articles.summary: Highlighting how India has maintained close ties with its partners in the Pacific Ocean, Union Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Thursday posted a picture with his counterparts, Japanese Minister of Defense Shinjirō Koizumi, and the Australian Minister for Defence Richard Marles. "JAI: Japan, Australia, India", the Defence Minister posted on X, with him holding hands of both Marles and Koizumi, as he stood in the middle.  Earlier on Wednesday, Singh held a meeting with Koizumi on the sidelines of the 13th ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) in Cebu, the Philippines, and discussed ways to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation.In a post on X, Singh said, "Happy to meet with the Minister of Defense of Japan, Mr. Koizumi Shinjiro, on the sidelines of the 13th ADMM-Plus in Cebu, Philippines."Highlighting the importance of cooperation between the two countries, the Defence Minister said, "Our shared commitment remains vital for a free, open, and peaceful Indo-Pacific region."Koizumi also thanked Rajnath Singh for the warm welcome and the meeting. He assured of Japan's commitment to strengthening cooperation between the two countries across various areas, including defence.On the same day, Singh held a bilateral meeting with Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Richard Marles.In a post on X, Singh said the meeting provided an opportunity to review bilateral defence cooperation and discuss ways to strengthen coordination between the two countries.Emphasising the importance of bilateral ties, Singh said, "India places great value on its Comprehensive Strategic Partnership with Australia for a free, open, and secure Indo-Pacific."Both leaders also exchanged gifts as a gesture of goodwill and friendship. During the meeting, Singh also invited Marles to attend Aero India-2027, scheduled to be held in Bengaluru in February 2027.The ADMM is the highest defence consultative and cooperative mechanism in ASEAN. ADMM-Plus is a platform for ASEAN member states (Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Timor-Leste and Vietnam) and its eight Dialogue Partners (India, US, China, Russia, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand) to strengthen security and defence cooperation.

articles.title: Samsung logs $80.5b profit despite AI jitters
articles.summary: Seoul: Massive demand for AI chips delivered record quarterly profits to South Korea's Samsung Electronics on Thursday, but shares fell as investors questioned the resilience of the global tech boom.Samsung is the world's largest maker of memory chips -- components in short supply as advanced types are snapped up for use in data centres powering artificial intelligence.Also read: South Korea fines Google, Apple a combined $47.6 million over app store payment practicesThe company posted July-September operating profit at 107.4 trillion won ($80.5 billion) -- up more than 780 percent on-year.It marked the first time any technology company had reported quarterly operating profit over 100 trillion won, Samsung said.Net profit jumped more than 510 percent from last year to 75.1 trillion won, while sales reached 195.3 trillion won.The global race to build data centres to train and run chatbots, image generators and other AI tools has turbocharged the fortunes of Samsung and other chipmakers, despite concerns that the sector may be overvalued.Samsung shares fell more than five percent on Thursday morning.Investors were disappointed by a miss of market expectations for operating profit by the semiconductor division, according to Bloomberg News.The company's memory business achieved "another record-breaking quarter by managing its product mix, with a focus on AI products, amid capacity constraints," Samsung said in a statement."Strong demand momentum for servers led to higher market prices across all applications."'Unprecedented growth'Demand-driven shortages of advanced memory chips known as HBM, used in AI systems alongside other data-crunching semiconductors, has caused their price to spike.Dilin Wu, research strategist at Pepperstone, said strong earnings from Samsung and South Korean industry rival SK hynix were "a reminder that the AI memory boom is still very real, despite all the concerns we've seen around the broader AI trade"."Chipmakers are benefiting directly from the AI investment boom, while the companies buying their chips are still trying to prove they can earn a decent return on all that spending," she told AFP earlier this week.With sky-high expectations for stellar results, record profits may not be enough to reassure market players."Ultimately, investors want to know whether there's still another leg to this memory upcycle, or whether we're getting close to peak earnings," Wu said.Samsung predicted Thursday that it would continue to feel the benefits of the AI boom.Chief financial officer Park Soon-cheol told an earnings call the company expects "unprecedented growth in memory demand in 2027, driven by accelerating competition to build AI infrastructure and the expansion of personal AI agents"."On the supply side, however, we expect difficulties in expanding... output in a short period of time through new capacity additions," he said.Chip companies focusing their efforts on profitable HBM has also fuelled shortages of the less glamorous computer memory components used in everyday consumer electronics -- driving up the price of smartphones and laptops.Shareholder returnsSamsung on Thursday detailed plans to return up to 110 trillion won to shareholders this year, including 30 trillion won in cash dividends, following an August announcement.Record profits driven by booming demand for AI memory chips have fuelled calls for greater shareholder returns, particularly after shares in tech giants such as Samsung tumbled from their June record highs amid concerns over US tech firms' AI spending.The announcement comes a day after SK hynix also announced plans to return 60 trillion won to shareholders, following the completion of a 40 trillion-won shareholder return programme.Such shareholder returns "would allow the benefits of earnings growth to translate into greater shareholder returns," said Kim Dong-won, head of KB Securities' research center."With record profits and undervaluation coexisting, the largest-ever expansion of shareholder returns would be a decisive opportunity to address the company's undervaluation and serve as a key driver of a reassessment of its market value," said Kim.

Gold FoF Curbs: What investors can do now?
articles.summary: Several mutual fund houses have temporarily stopped accepting fresh investments into gold fund-of-funds (FoFs), leaving investors wondering whether they can continue investing through existing SIPs and what alternatives are available. Here is what the restrictions mean and what investors can do if they still want exposure to gold.WHAT ARE GOLD FUND-OF-FUNDS (FOFs), AND HOW DO THEY WORK?Gold FoFs are mutual fund schemes that invest in Gold ETFs rather than buying physical gold directly.When an investor puts money into a Gold FoF, the fund manager uses that money to purchase units of a Gold ETF. The Gold ETF, in turn, invests in physical gold. As a result, a Gold FoF’s value generally moves in line with gold prices.They offer a simple way to invest in gold through the mutual fund route without needing a demat account. Investors can buy and redeem units like any other mutual fund scheme while gaining exposure to changes in gold prices.WHY HAVE SOME MUTUAL FUND HOUSES RESTRICTED FRESH INVESTMENTS IN GOLD FOFs?Several fund houses have temporarily stopped accepting fresh investments in Gold FoFs from mid-October. The restrictions include fresh lump-sum investments, new SIP registrations and switch-ins, though they differ across schemes.While fund houses have not disclosed specific reasons behind the move, industry participants believe it may be linked to concerns over rising gold imports and strong inflows into gold investment products. As these ETF units are backed by physical gold, sustained inflows into such products can translate into higher demand for imported gold.Read more: Best gilt mutual funds to invest in October 2026CAN’T INVEST IN A GOLD FOF? WHAT ARE THE OTHER OPTIONS?Gold ETFs are one of the closest alternatives for investors seeking exposure to gold through market-linked investments. While there are restrictions on fresh investments in several Gold FoFs, there are none on their ETFs.Read more: Top 8 equity MFs offer double-digit gains on SIP investments since last Diwali. Do you own any?HOW ARE GOLD ETFs DIFFERENT FROM GOLD FOFs?Gold FoFs are generally more convenient for retail investors because they can be bought and redeemed like any other mutual fund scheme without requiring a demat account. Gold ETFs can only be bought and sold through a demat and trading account.Gold ETFs typically have lower costs because investors bear only the ETF’s expense ratio. In a Gold FoF, investors indirectly bear the expenses of both the FoF and the underlying ETF.Liquidity also differs. Gold ETFs can be bought and sold on stock exchanges during market hours, while Gold FoFs are purchased and redeemed at the day’s closing net asset value (NAV), like regular mutual funds.However, unlike Gold FoFs, their ETFs do not offer the convenience of a mutual fund SIP. Though many brokers have SIP facilities for buying ETFs and stocks, they are perceived to be relatively less user-friendly. Also, not all ETFs are liquid. Some of them might be trading at a premium to the ETF’s NAV.
